nameStory: The Flat Crep gets its name from its distinctly flattened, shelf-like appearance that lacks the typical mushroom stem. 'Crep' comes from the genus name Crepidotus, which means 'slipper-like' in Latin, referring to how these fungi often look like little slippers attached to wood. The 'flat' part is obvious once you see one - they're pressed against their woody homes like pancakes stuck to a tree!
description: Flat Creps are small, bracket-like fungi that grow directly from dead wood without a visible stem. They look like tiny brown or tan shelves, usually no bigger than a silver dollar, projecting horizontally from logs and branches. These little oysterlings belong to a group of fungi that specialize in decomposing dead hardwood, and they're quite common once you know what to look for. Their flat, fan-shaped caps and brownish spore deposits make them distinctive among the small wood-dwelling fungi.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small, flat, and shelf-like, ranging from light tan to brown, with a kidney or fan shape that attaches directly to wood without a stem

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Radiating from the attachment point like a fan, starting whitish but becoming brown as spores mature, feeling soft to the touch

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Brown to rusty-brown color - you can see this as a dusty coating on surfaces below older specimens

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and slightly fuzzy when fresh, becoming papery and brittle as it dries out

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from dead hardwood with no stem, often in overlapping clusters like tiny brown shingles

habitat: Look for Flat Creps on dead branches and logs of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, especially on oak, maple, and beech. They prefer wood that's been dead for a while but isn't completely rotten yet. You'll often find them on fallen branches in mixed hardwood forests, from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Fresh specimens begin appearing on overwintered deadwood as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture for fungal growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when you'll find the most fresh, soft specimens after summer thunderstorms provide the moisture these fungi need.
seasonality.fall: Still producing new fruiting bodies, especially during wet autumn weather, though many specimens from earlier in the year will be dried and papery.
seasonality.winter: Old dried specimens persist on wood and are still identifiable, though no new growth occurs during freezing weather.

funFact: Despite being tiny and inconspicuous, Flat Creps are wood recycling champions that can completely break down dead branches over several years, turning solid wood into rich soil nutrients that feed the forest - one small shelf fungus can process many times its own weight in dead wood!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small oysterlings in the same genus, but Flat Creps are consistently more flattened and lack any hint of a stem. Remember: truly FLAT Creps are the Flat Creps - if it has any stem-like attachment, look for other Crepidotus species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'oysterling' refers to small oyster mushroom relatives that grow on wood, but unlike true oyster mushrooms, oysterlings have brown spores instead of white ones. This spore color difference is a key family trait that separates the Crepidotaceae from the Pleurotaceae (true oyster mushroom family).
compareHints: Flat Crep is the most consistently stemless species in its genus - while other oysterlings like the Peeling Oysterling or Variable Oysterling might have small stems or be more cup-shaped, Flat Crep lives up to its name by being genuinely flat against the wood. The brown spore print distinguishes all Crepidotus species from the white-spored true oyster mushrooms that might grow nearby on similar substrates.
